summary: States the Work-Energy Principle (W_net = delta K.E.), derives it from Newton's Second Law and the third equation of motion, interprets positive/negative/zero net work, and works a numeric example calculating net work from initial and final kinetic energy.
title: 5.3 Work-Energy Principle

topicTitle: 5.2 Work Done by a Constant and Variable Force
summary: Defines work as the dot product W = Fd*cos(theta) for a constant force, covers when work is positive, negative, or zero, and explains that for a variable force (like a spring), work must be found as the area under a Force-Displacement (or Force-Extension) graph, or via the integral W = integral of F dd.
title: Work Done by a Constant and Variable Force

summary: Defines kinetic energy K.E. = (1/2)mv^2, derives it from Newton's Second Law and the equations of motion, expresses it in terms of momentum as K.E. = p^2/(2m), and states the Work-Energy Theorem W_net = delta K.E., including its form when a resistive medium removes energy as heat.
title: Introduction

summary: Defines gravitational (P.E. = mgh) and elastic ((1/2)kx^2) potential energy as stored energy due to position or deformation, and distinguishes conservative forces (path-independent, allow potential energy to be defined, e.g. gravity, springs) from non-conservative forces (path-dependent, dissipate energy, e.g. friction), explaining why mechanical energy is conserved only when non-conservative forces are absent.
title: Potential Energy (P.E.)

summary: Defines absolute gravitational potential energy U_g = -GMm/r with the zero reference at infinite distance, derives this formula via a telescoping sum of small work increments, and explains why U_g is always negative and how it relates to the mgh approximation used near Earth's surface.
title: Absolute Gravitational Potential Energy

topicTitle: 5.6 Work Done in a Gravitational Field
summary: Defines gravitational field strength g = GM/r^2, explains what makes a field conservative (path-independent work, zero work over closed paths), and proves gravity is conservative by showing the work done between two points is the same along a straight and a curved path, and zero around any closed loop.
title: Work Done in a Gravitational Field

topicTitle: 5.7 Interconversion of Kinetic and Potential Energy
summary: Explains how kinetic and potential energy convert into each other while total mechanical energy (K.E. + P.E.) stays constant under conservative forces, illustrated with a freely falling object (v = sqrt(2gh)) and a swinging pendulum, and shows how friction breaks the conservation by converting some energy into heat.
title: Interconversion of Kinetic and Potential Energy

topicTitle: 5.8 Work-Energy Principle in a Resistive Medium
summary: Extends the Work-Energy Principle to include resistive forces (friction, air resistance), which always do negative work (W_resistive = -F*d), showing W_net = W_applied + W_resistive = delta K.E., derives mgh = (1/2)mv^2 + fh for a body falling through resistance, and solves a numeric example combining applied force and friction.
title: Work-Energy Principle in a Resistive Medium

summary: Defines power P = W/t as the rate of doing work, covers its units (watt, kilowatt, horsepower), distinguishes average from instantaneous power, derives P = F.v, and clarifies that the kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy (3.6 x 10^6 J), not power.
title: Power

summary: Defines efficiency as the ratio of useful output to total input energy or power, explains why real machines are always below 100% efficiency, and covers the Carnot engine's theoretical maximum efficiency eta = 1 - T_sink/T_source, worked with the freezing/boiling point example (~26.8%).
title: 5.5 Efficiency

summary: Defines escape velocity as the minimum speed to break free from a planet's gravity, derives v_esc = sqrt(2GM/R) from energy conservation (total mechanical energy = 0), gives the equivalent form v_esc = sqrt(2gR) using surface gravity, and calculates Earth's escape velocity as approximately 11.2 km/s.
title: Escape Velocity

summary: Surveys five non-conventional (renewable) energy sources: tidal energy (dams harnessing tidal rise/fall), wave energy (devices like Salter's Duck), solar energy (thermal collectors and photovoltaic cells), geothermal energy (heat from hot springs, geysers, and hot rocks), and biomass (stored solar energy in organic matter).
title: Non-Conventional Energy Sources

summary: Defines biomass as stored solar energy in organic matter and covers the three main conversion methods: direct combustion (burning for heat/steam), fermentation (producing ethanol biofuel), and biogas production (anaerobic digestion yielding methane biogas and fertilizer slurry).
title: Biomass Energy

summary: Explains geothermal energy as heat from radioactive decay, residual planetary heat, and compression, covers how it is harnessed via natural manifestations (hot springs, geysers, fumaroles), electricity generation as a heat engine (W = Q_H - Q_C), and Hot Dry Rock direct heating, and discusses energy degradation and environmental impact on geysers.
title: Geothermal Energy
